assessment.nobel_worthiness: Political economics gave a unified framework, from theory to systematic empirics, for how electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and fiscal institutions shape policy and development. It opened a field that is now standard across economics and political science, and it is deep, widely cited and policy-relevant.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini built the constitutional and electoral-rules program, with their joint textbook and papers. Besley, often with Persson, developed state capacity and the empirical political economy of institutions. A three-person prize is coherent and the core credit is clear, though others such as Alesina, Acemoglu and Robinson also work nearby.
assessment.maturity: The work spans roughly three decades and has been thoroughly tested and extended. Timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2024 institutions prize may weigh against a near-term recognition of political economy.
Whether the committee would prefer a narrower core, or add other political economists, is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural demand estimation with differentiated products (BLP) and dynamic industry models (Ericson-Pakes) turned industrial organisation into a quantitative discipline. The methods are now used routinely in merger review, antitrust and regulation, which is a clear methodological and practical impact.
assessment.attribution: The BLP contribution is clearly Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. Pakes also led the dynamic framework and the estimation methods. Bresnahan, Benkard and others are important but more peripheral to the core.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1990s and has been validated by decades of use and refinement.
uncertainties: Excluding Bresnahan and other contributors may be contested.
Strong IO and econometrics contributions could be split across several fields.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints and credit cycles explain how small shocks are amplified and persist through balance sheets. The framework is foundational for modern macro-finance and was vindicated by the 2008 crisis.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) is the core, cleanly attributable contribution. Gertler and Gilchrist form a distinct financial-accelerator line, and Bernanke's prior recognition complicates that branch. A two-person prize is the most defensible.
assessment.maturity: Nearly thirty years of validation. Applications have grown since the financial crisis.
uncertainties: The Bernanke-Diamond-Dybvig 2022 prize may overlap in the committee's mind.
The credit of Gertler in this line versus the New Keynesian line is ambiguous.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting transformed how trade economists understand the gains from trade, with the intensive and extensive margins and reallocation effects. It had a large empirical and theoretical impact and reoriented the field after the Krugman prize.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman is the long-standing theoretical architect of the new trade theory. Redding's role is substantial but more quantitative and later.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of use, with strong empirical support and a large literature.
uncertainties: Whether Bernard, Eaton and Kortum deserve credit alongside Melitz.
Quantitative trade models (B044) are close relatives and could compete for the same slot.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, with nominal rigidities, micro-founded monetary policy and the Taylor rule, underpins how central banks think and model. It is highly influential in policy practice and macro theory.
assessment.attribution: The credit is widely diffused, among Woodford, Gali, Taylor, Calvo, Clarida, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Smets and Wouters, among others. Any three-person selection is open to dispute. Woodford's synthesis and Gali's formulation are the strongest candidates.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, and its limitations have been exposed by the inflation surge of 2021-23 and by heterogeneous-agent critiques.
uncertainties: Severe attribution diffusion makes a clean three-person prize hard.
Recent policy performance may colour views of the framework.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run top-income and wealth data series reshaped empirical and policy discussion of inequality worldwide. The data and measurement contribution is substantial, though some theoretical interpretation, such as r>g, is contested.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez built the top-income series. Zucman extended the work to offshore wealth and distributional national accounts. Atkinson, now deceased, was a key predecessor and collaborator.
assessment.maturity: The core work is about 20 years old and has been replicated across countries, but methodological debates remain on measurement, for example on tax-data treatment.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes over wealth estimates and the r>g mechanism.
Public and policy prominence may not match scientific consensus.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Misallocation analysis offers a quantitative account of cross-country income differences through the efficiency of resource allocation across firms. It has been very influential in growth and development accounting and links to the growth themes recognised in recent prizes.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) is the central paper, with Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) as a parallel contribution. Restuccia is a defensible third laureate, but a two-person prize is cleanest.
assessment.maturity: About fifteen years of work with a large literature, though the interpretation of measured misallocation and measurement error remain debated.
uncertainties: Measurement error and the interpretation of dispersion in marginal products are debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population administrative data transformed measurement of intergenerational mobility and of place effects. It combines large-scale data innovation with credible causal designs and has strong policy relevance.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the dominant figure. Hendren and Friedman are important co-authors, with Katz connected to the Moving to Opportunity work. Credit within a large team is hard to apportion.
assessment.maturity: The work is relatively recent, from about 2014 onward. Replication and long-run assessment are still developing, so it is early.
uncertainties: Timing may be premature compared with the more established candidates.
Team-based credit is diffuse, and some findings on place effects are still being tested.
